commons:28968893.summary: Christ sits in a round glory carried aloft by four angels, two above and two flying beneath, his right hand raised in blessing. Below, the Virgin stands at the centre with her hands raised, flanked by the apostles, who gaze and gesture upward. In the Byzantine tradition the Ascension shows both Christ's departure in glory and the Church, gathered around his Mother, left to await his return.
facts: The plaque was once the central panel of a small folding triptych, as the Berlin museum's title for it records (inv. 580).
It is catalogued as a Byzantine ('Eastern Roman') work of the second half of the 11th century.
commons:28968893.notes: Facts are from the Commons description and the SMB record title linked from it; the SMB online collection (record 1892163) could not be loaded for confirmation during this review. The material is assumed to be ivory from the file's categories (Byzantine ivory in the Bode-Museum).

commons:89497895.summary: Against the gold ground the young, beardless Christ, robed in purple with a jewelled cross-nimbus, stretches out his hand towards the possessed man who crouches before a rocky outcrop, while a disciple in white raises his hand in witness. To the right, the swine into which the unclean spirits were sent plunge down into the blue water. With a handful of figures the mosaicist tells the whole story of Christ's authority over the powers of evil.
facts: It is one of the thirteen miracle and teaching scenes in the topmost register of the nave, made under Theodoric in the early 6th century; in all of them Christ appears young and beardless.
Three of the swine are shown in the water, a compact visual shorthand for the herd of the Gospel account.

commons:89497895.notes: Not otherwise present in the collection (other Sant'Apollinare Nuovo scenes are). Date follows the Theodorican campaign as used for the companion scenes (c. 500–526).

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-143-chris.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, flanked by angels, bends down in an inclined mandorla — 'bow thy heavens, O Lord, and come down' — and hands the armoured psalmist a sword and shield. Angels touch the mountains so that they smoke and hurl spears at an armoured host, and at the far right the psalmist appears again with a harp, singing a new song. 'Blessed be the Lord my strength, which teacheth my hands to war' frames the scene.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-143-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:objects-berlin-gilded-crucifixion-iv.summary: Within an arched frame whose columns and canopy still carry much of their gilding, Christ hangs on the cross with a golden halo, flanked by the Virgin and St John, with angels in the upper corners. The well-preserved gold gives a rare idea of how luminous these ivories originally appeared. The serene body of Christ, alive in death, expresses the Byzantine understanding of the Crucifixion as victory.
facts: Gilding and paint once covered parts of many Byzantine ivories; this relief preserves unusually extensive traces of it (type).

wga:zearly/1/1sculptu/various/7statue1.summary: A youthful, beardless shepherd in a short belted tunic, leggings and boots, with a satchel at his side, carries a lamb across his shoulders, holding its legs in his hands and gazing calmly outward. The figure was originally carved in high relief on a sarcophagus decorated with pastoral scenes, found in the Catacomb of Callixtus on the Appian Way, and was cut free and completed as an independent statuette in 1764. Though much restored, this gentle figure is one of the best-loved images of early Christian Rome, giving almost three-dimensional form to the image that dominated Christian art before Constantine: Christ the shepherd who goes after the lost sheep and carries it home rejoicing.
facts: It entered the papal collections in 1764, when it was sold for the Christian Museum of Pope Benedict XIV; the restorers of that time recarved or replaced parts of the head, the arms, one leg, the lamb's legs and the back.
The museum that houses it today was founded by Pope Pius IX in 1854 to preserve finds from the Roman catacombs that could not be kept in their original sites.
The pose follows the ancient Greek 'kriophoros' (ram-bearer) type, a figure long associated with Hermes; Christians adopted it with new meaning.
Early Christians largely avoided free-standing statues, which were associated with pagan cult images; the shepherd's origin as a sarcophagus relief reflects this preference for relief carving.
The shepherd's short tunic is the working dress of a Roman herdsman, not royal or priestly robes: Christ is shown as one who serves.
